title: Epoch-based affinity and cross-tier fallback orchestration for rolling model upgrades
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Current rollout semantics (canary / A-B) + model version pinning interact poorly with multi-dimensional routing (region selection and tiered capacity). We see either: 1) strict pinning that prevents graceful degradation when a region or tier is saturated, or 2) overly permissive fallbacks that silently change model variant during a user session and break KV cache/ordering assumptions. This ticket defines an approach we call 'epoch-based affinity' plus a cross-tier fallback orchestration to reconcile pinning guarantees with production reliability needs.

Goals:
- Preserve strong version-affinity within a logical session/epoch while allowing safe degradations when capacity or region constraints trigger fallback.
- Avoid unexpected model switches mid-request or mid-conversation that invalidate KV caches.
- Provide predictable SLO behavior and observable metrics during rollouts across regions and tiers.

High-level approach:
1) Epoch-based affinity: bind requests to an "epoch id" tied to a user-session token or a short-lived routing cookie. The epoch carries (model_version, epoch_start_ts, affinity_ttl). Affinity TTL is coarse-grained and aligns with rollout windows (e.g., 30m, 2h).
2) Graceful downgrade policy at routing layer: when the target route is unavailable (region outage, tier saturation, quota), the router evaluates a deterministic fallback sequencer that prefers: same model family on lower tier -> smaller quantized variant -> compatible model variant in same family -> compatible variant in different family (with semantic compatibility hints).
3) KV cache migration guard: if a downgrade would change model parameterization enough to invalidate cache (model_family changes or different tokenizer/embedding), the router will either (a) allow a one-time rebind at epoch boundary with session-level notification or (b) route to a fallback in a different region that preserves cache compatibility, depending on cost/latency tradeoffs.
4) Canary split semantics: For canary cohorts we maintain rollout affinity by mapping epoch bins to rollout cohorts deterministically (hash(user_id) mod N) so users maintain stable exposure during TTL; canary weight changes are applied at cohort boundaries only.

Acceptance criteria:
- Routing service can attach and persist epoch metadata for request-scoped routing decisions.
- Router implements sequencer of fallback candidates and can express compatibility metadata for each variant.
- Integration tests that simulate region/tier failure confirm: no in-flight request experiences a mid-token model switch; session-level affinity is honored within TTL; fallback path logs/metrics are emitted.
- Dashboard: rollout cohort stability, epoch churn rate, fallback frequency, KV cache invalidation events, and latency/cost delta for fallback paths.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Longer affinity TTL reduces churn but slows rollout speed and delays canary exposure. We need TTL tuning heuristics.
- Complexity increase in routing layer and metadata propagation to edge. Requires schema change in request routing header.
- Potential cost increase when preferring cross-region routing to preserve cache compatibility.

Open design decisions:
- Default affinity TTL for user sessions vs. API keys (interactive chat vs. batch jobs). Proposal: 30 minutes for interactive sessions, 5 minutes for short API requests, configurable per-route.
- Whether to surface explicit session-level notification on fallback (e.g., response header or structured event) vs. silent transition logged to observability.

Notes on compatibility metadata: each model variant in the catalog must publish: model_family_id, tokenizer_hash, kv_cache_compatibility_id, approximate_latency_profile, tier_hint. This metadata will drive sequencer decisions.
